newsitem.title: UK: Perry tells Iraq's Saddam to move A-A missiles.
newsitem.headline: Perry tells Iraq's Saddam to move A-A missiles.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry on Monday warned Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein to stop deploying anti-aircraft missile batteries in the extended southern Iraqi no-fly zone or face the consequences.

Perry issued the warning after briefing British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo and French Defence Minister Charles Millon on talks he had in Bahrain, Kuwait, Turkey and Saudi Arabia over the continuing crisis.

"Saddam Hussein poses a threat to our airmen, not only by the six missile firings carried out in the past days but also by the aggressive deployment of mobile surface-to-air missile units ... in the southern sector," Perry told reporters.
"All of these actions we find threatening, we find provoking and we find necessary he change," Perry added.
Perry said President Clinton had warned the Iraqi leader that the Western allies reserved the right to take any action they saw fit "and our position still stands."
The U.S.-led offensive against Saddam has split the Gulf War coalition. Some members have expressed severe doubts about U.S. bombing raids.
But Portillo said France, the United States and Britain -- whose pilots are patrolling the no-fly zone -- were united in their determination to prevent Saddam's forces from threatening their planes.
"We think it is very important for Saddam Hussein to understand that he should not take actions which affect the safety of the men flying those planes," Portillo said.
Perry said all three nations had agreed that the policy of containing Saddam was of paramount importance.
"All of our actions have been carried out with the support of our allies in the region," he insisted.
In Washington, Clinton said the United States sought no confrontation with Iraq but he declined to rule out air strikes.

"We have sought no confrontation with Saddam Hussein," Clinton replied when asked if Iraq's decision to stop firing at allied jets policing Iraqi no-fly zones meant Washington could forego any immediate air strikes.

At the Pentagon, Army General John Shalikashvili said U.S. intelligence was still getting "mixed" signals on Iraq's air defence movements in the south and Washington would continue its build-up, including plans to send 3,000 or more troops to Kuwait from Fort Hood, Texas.
"We are not standing down," said Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. "Whether air strikes will be necessary or not will very much depend Saddam Hussein's actions, not his words."
